utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Registrar, could you call the case number, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good day, Mr. President. Case number IT-04-74-T, the Prosecutor versus Prlic et al.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. Registrar. On the last day of August, 31 of August, 2006, I would like to greet everyone present in the courtroom. I would like to greet Mr. Mundis and his assistants, all the members of the Defence counsel, the accused. Mr. Prlic [as interpreted] will be joining us soon. As far as I know he's on his way, but he is assisted by his counsel, so he will be joining us soon. Yesterday, Mr. Karnavas posed two questions, one that concerned article 71 -- Rule 71. Mr. Karnavas requested that we implement this procedure for the witness who will be appearing on Monday. The Judges have discussed the matter, and we won't grant this request, which means that the witness who will be heard on Monday will appear as scheduled. Having taken the solemn declaration he will answer the questions put to him by the Prosecution with regard to his expert report, and he will also be cross-examined. And the second point Mr. Karnavas says as follows, and this is the Chamber's position: You mentioned an Article 91(H)(ii). When the Defence has a document that might contradict testimony of a witness, but the question, the relevant question wasn't put to the witness by the Prosecution, the question was, if the Defence doesn't present this document or -- if the Defence doesn't mention the subject, does that mean that they no longer have the right to return to that question. Mr. Karnavas then said that there were two systems that one could follow. There was the American system and the Australian one. In the Australian and British system it is prohibited to return to such a subject. The Judge is a lot more flexible, and in our opinion if the issue hasn't been mentioned it may be mentioned, it may be referred to at a subsequent date. So, Mr. Karnavas, I want you to be reassured as far as that is concerned. Those are the two issues I wanted to mention.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... had planned and this would have been in the name of the Chamber also to comment on the behaviour of Mr. Karnavas yesterday as found in the transcript on page 79 on lines 3 and 4 but I do not think it would be correct to make such an observation in his absence, so I will postpone this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Mr. Mundis, we have a witness who is waiting. I see that we have some protective measures. There's a blind there. Is there any issue you would like to debate? We'll move into private session.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We're in open session, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm waiting to see the little symbol on the screen, the little rectangle. Yes. It's fine. Sir, you will first have to answer the questions put to you by the individuals you met yesterday. They will take one hour to put their questions to you. We will then have a 20-minute break, after which you will have to answer the questions put to you by Defence counsel. You might think that there are a lot of them, but there is only one Defence lawyer for each accused. They will put their questions to you. It's also possible that two of the accused might intervene to put technical questions to you. And the four Judges sitting before you might also put questions to you in order to obtain more precise answers to some of your testimony or in order to find out more about the events that you are a witness of and events that are referred to in the indictment and that we believe are important. If you run into any difficulties, don't hesitate to inform us of the fact, and rest assured things should run smoothly. This has always been the case, so you have no reason for concern. I'll now give the floor to the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Good morning, Witness BL.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: In response to one of my questions earlier, sir, you told us that you were there the village of Lapsunj. Can you tell the Trial Chamber until what year you lived in that village?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I lived in that village up until the war.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Can you tell the Trial Chamber, sir, about the background, that is the ethnic background or composition of the village at the time the war started?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Muslims and four or five Croatian households lived in the village, whereas the neighbouring villages were Croatian.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: And approximately -- again, sir, focusing on 1991, 1992, approximately Muslim households were there in the village of Lapsunj?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: About 60.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: In which opstina is Lapsunj located?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In Prozor municipality.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Can you describe for the Trial Chamber the relations between the Muslims and Croats in the village of Lapsunj up until the spring of 1992?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The relations were excellent. We went to each other's marriages, everything was fine. There were never any problems.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Mr. President, for the record the Prosecution notes that the accused, Mr. Pusic, has now entered the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Witness BL, can you please tell us what happened commencing in April of 1992?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I worked in a company until 1992, until April, and then I was mobilised by the TO, the Territorial Defence. I responded to the call-up papers, and we went to Prozor, reported to them, and they sent us to the hydroelectric power plant Rama in a vehicle. They distributed to weapons to us and equipment. They took us then to -- they took us to Ravasnica and that is where we had to establish positions. We stayed there for a while because the shift was a 15-day shift, and I was a little late in responding to the call-up, so I spent between 7 and 10 days up there.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Let me interrupt you there, Witness BL. When you say that you were on these positions near Ravasnica, who was at these positions? Who were you manning these positions with, and against whom?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We were there with HVO, and we were facing the Serbs.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: And again, Witness BL, when you say "we," "We were there with the HVO," to whom does the pronoun "we" refer?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We, the Muslims, most of the people who were there.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Were the Muslims at this point in April, 1992, organised into any type of military formation or structure?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They were in the form of the Territorial Defence. There was a Joint Command.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: And again, Witness BL, for purposes of clarity, when you say there was a Joint Command, what forces were part of this Joint Command?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: At the time, it was the HVO and the army or, rather, the TO.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Armija, interpreter's correction.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] When you were there against the Serbs, did you have a uniform with insignia? What sort of insignia did you have?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I personally didn't have any insignia at the time, but the HVO had provided me with a uniform.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And there was no insignia of any kind on the uniform?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And did you have a commander?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, at the time, yes, of course we had a commander.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And did the commander have a uniform with insignia?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't know. I wouldn't see the commander.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You don't know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: If I may go on a little. You said you have not seen the commander. Was there no one who gave orders that you have seen?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. I couldn't see the one at the top. [French on English channel].

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: I am not now referring to the man at the top but the man or woman -- [French on English channel].

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] When I went to Ravasnica, there was a man I didn't know from the Rama Brigade.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: And was this service something you had been trained for before together with those that you were together with there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] As in the JNA, I had been in a -- in a recoilless gun crew. They called on me, and we were setting up recoilless guns there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Am I right to suppose that you were -- or to understand you as saying that you were trained in the JNA previously?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, because I served in the JNA.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Excuse me, Mr. Mundis.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. There's another question from the Judges and then we'll give the floor back to Mr. Mundis.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness BL following along -- BL. Yes, BL. Following along from that stream of thought, with regards to your military service, you said whether it was a battalion or company, every day or every week after doing your service did you have a military camp or did you go back to your own house with your weapons, taking your weapons with you? Was there any military rule, a clear-cut military rule that you had to follow in that respect, and were there any military tribunals at the time for anyone who transgressed the rules? Could you answer that, please? And of course when I'm talking about you, I mean Muslims as HVO members. So I'm talking about where the military people were put up and military rules as applied to that armed group and military jurisdiction to give me an idea of the discipline that existed with respect to these groups at the time.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Of course there was a military institution there on the side of the HVO, but the shifts lasted 15 days. We spent the nights at Zahum near Ravasnica. After the 15-day shift we would go home. There would be a shift change.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So you would go home, and would you take your weapons with you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, we did. The light weapons, not the heavy ones.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Did you belong to the Rama Brigade in fact?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I did at that time. At that time, I was attached from the TO brigade to the Rama Brigade.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Mr. Mundis, thanks to those questions. We're much clearer now.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Witness BL, during the time period 1992, 1993, did you hold any military rank or command responsibility at any level?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I was a private. I didn't have any rank or any important duty.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Witness BL, I would like to turn your attention now to the period in late June, 1993. Late June, 1993. At that point in time, did you continue having any military duties or responsibilities?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The question is not clear to me. Could you please explain it a little bit.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Witness BL, where were you on June 26th, 1993?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We were at Idovac. I was at the line at Idovac with the HVO facing the Serbs, and we were up there, and it was the end of the shift. We were doing 7/7, then. Sometimes it was 7/15. And the end of the shift arrived and news came that some lads from the village of Lapsunj had fled through Drasevo towards Gornji Vakuf, and then they told us that we should go home. We handed in our weapons, and they said we would no longer be coming to the front line because they didn't trust us, because they thought that we had let those lads pass through the line.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Sorry. Witness BL, let me interrupt you there to ask some questions of clarification. Where is Idovac?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Idovac is between Kupres, Gornji Vakuf, and Prozor at the meeting of the three border lines.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: In which opstina is Idovac locate the?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Prozor.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Approximately how far is Idovac from Lapsunj?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't know. I only have eight years of primary school, of elementary school. I can't tell you how many kilometres.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Now, sir, you mentioned, "We were doing 7/7 then. Sometimes it was 7/15." And that's page 14, line 14. Can you tell the Trial Chamber what you mean by 7/7 or 7/15?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We were at the lines. Sometimes we would spend seven days at the line and seven days at home, or 15 days at the line and seven days at home. It depended. It changed with time.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: In response just a few moments ago to a question from Judge Mindua, you told him that you kept your weapons, you small arms. On this day, however, you told us that you handed in your weapons. Was that the normal procedure in June, 1993?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, no, because in June, on the 26th, we gave that back. But after the attack on Prozor, then weapons began to be handed back to the HVO.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Now, sir, can you tell the Trial Chamber where you went on the 26th of June, 1993, after handing in your weapons?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: When we handed in our weapons, we went to Prozor in trucks. They put us in the firemens' club, in a small room in the basement. It was 2 by 4 metres, something like that. It couldn't have been bigger. And we stayed there, and they said we would just have to make some kind of statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Okay. Witness BL, again let me interrupt you. When you say, "We handed in our weapons," who is "we"?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We the Muslims who were up there.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: And how -- who was driving these trucks? You say, "We went to Prozor in trucks." Who was driving the trucks?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Members of the HVO from the civilian protection. I have no idea who was driving.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Where is this firemen's club that you've made reference to?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It's -- coming from Jablanica, it's just when you enter Prozor.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: How many of you were in the group that were taken to the firemen's club?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: There were about 25 of us in the fire station.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: And how long did you remain in the fire station?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We only spent the night there. And in the morning, one or two, or I don't know how many soldiers came in, and they said they needed a few men to do some work. And then they put us on trucks and took us in the direction of Uzdol.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Let me -- sorry, Witness BL.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: I would ask, Mr. President, with the assistance of the usher that the witness be shown a photograph, which we have a hard copy of here. Or it's also in e-court. It bears Exhibit number P 9683. This is one of the photographs that was in the site visit book. 9683.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Witness, do you see a photograph on the screen in front of you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I do. That's the photograph -- the building.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: What building do you see on the screen in front of you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It's the fire station.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: And this is the fire station where you were kept overnight?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Witness. Now, you told us at the point when I interrupted you, said at lines 15 and 16 of page 6, "They put us on trucks and took us in the direction of Uzdol." Who put you on trucks when you say, "They put us on trucks"?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The HVO soldiers, because the military police was there in the fire station, and they were the only ones who had contact with us there, and they allowed these soldiers to take us off to work in Uzdol.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Now, Witness BL, when you say the military police was there in the fire station, how do you know that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Because we saw them. They were the only ones who had contact with us.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Well, let me ask you this: How do you know they were military police?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We saw their belts and their uniforms.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Was there anything distinctive about their belts and uniforms?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, it was a camouflage uniform with white military police belts.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: These military police that you saw in the fires station, did they have any insignia on their uniforms?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't remember well. It wasn't easy for us to approach them and look at their insignia. We weren't at a country fair so that we could go and inspect people's insignia. We were in prison.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Which -- with which military force were these military police affiliated?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The HVO.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: How do you know that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Because at that time there was no BH army in Prozor, nor were there any uniforms either in the TO or anywhere. After the fall of Prozor, it was only the HVO that existed. The HVO ruled.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Witness BL, to go back to the subject you were telling us about, how many people were among the group that was taken to Uzdol or in the direction of Uzdol?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: There were 20 something. Only the chief person among us Muslims stayed behind, only one, so that they could talk to him, and all the rest of us went to work in the direction of Uzdol.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: And where were you taken on this day, in the last few days of June, 1993? Where did they take you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They took us to Uzdol, and we slept or spent the nights in the primary school. During the day we went to work at the line in Komin near Kapela.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Now, Witness BL, when you say, "We went to work at the line in Komin near Kapela," what type of work are you referring to?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We dug trenches, fortified the line, did channels. Everything that was needed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: And how long did you remain on the line in Komin near Kapela in the area of Uzdol?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We went there to work, and we stayed at the prison in Uzdol for 12 days. But every day we went to work at Komin.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: And after this period of 12 days when you were in Uzdol and Komin, where did you go?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Our wives were asking around to find out where we were, and then they sent us back home, and then every morning we had to report in the centre of Lapsunj village. We reported there for several days, and after that we went from home to work at Crni Vrh. After a while, this sent us back to the primary school in Prozor. When we were coming back from work, they accept us there in trucks.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Okay. Again --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: May I just ask a question which may appear stupid to you. I am aware of this, but I have to ask. Did you get any pay for the work you performed?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Witness BL, let me go back to the previous answer. During this time period when you were back home, you told us, "Every morning we had to report in the centre of Lapsunj village," lines 4 and 5, page 19. What did you do after you reported in the centre of Lapsunj village?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It's not clear to me. Could you clarify your question, please?

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: You told us, Witness BL, that you would report in the morning. "Every morning we had to report in the centre of Lapsunj village." What happened after you reported? Did you go home? Did you go somewhere else? What did you do after you reported in the morning during this period you were at home?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: For two or three days or I don't know how long we would rest, and then we would go to work at Crni Vrh. They took us there.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: And, Witness BL, what type of work did you do at Crni Vrh?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Dug trenches and fortified the lines and whatever else was necessary.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: You told us on lines 6 and 7 of page 19, "After a while they sent us back to the primary school in Prozor." Do you recall approximately when it was you were taken to the school in Prozor?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It was to the secondary school in Prozor. I am semi-literate. I can't remember every date or time. I can't remember hours and minutes. I'm not comfortable with that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Do you recall the approximate month and year when you were taken to the secondary school in Prozor?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: As far as I can recall, it was in July, 1993, but I really don't know the precise date.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Now, again, Mr. President, with the assistance of the usher I would ask that the witness be shown photograph P 9685. That's P 9685. Again, this is one of the photos from the site visit material.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's the secondary school.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Again, for the record, sir, this photo that you're looking at, can you tell us what it is and where it is?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't understand what you mean. Could you repeat your question.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Sorry. You just mentioned that's the secondly school. I take it from that that this photo depicts the secondary school?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: And in what town is that school located?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In Prozor, at the top of the town under Makljen hill.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Now, Witness BL, how long did you stay in the secondary school in Prozor?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I stayed there until the 31st of July, 1993.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Do you recall approximately how many days or how many nights you stayed in the secondary school in Prozor?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't, because every morning I was taken to work, and every evening I would just come there to spend the night. I didn't have a piece of paper and a pencil to note down dates, years, months, or the number of people.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Can you recall or can you give us any approximate number with respect to the amount of people that were in the secondary school in Prozor during the time period you were there in July, 1993?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I can't say exactly, but roughly there might have been about 10 classrooms and several people in them. About 500 people, I would say. But as I said a moment ago, I didn't count all the time there. I was in prison, and I was doing work.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Now, you said on page 21, line 11, "Every morning I was taken to work." Who took you to work?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, the HVO soldiers.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: And were you the only one that was taken to work?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: There were others too. A group would come and they would need 10, and then another group needed 20. Some groups would need 15. But as I was young at the time, and I'm not too old now, thank goodness, either, I was the first one they would take for work.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Now, Witness, you told us on line 24 of page 21 that the HVO soldiers took you to work. How do you know they were HVO soldiers?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Because they had insignia.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Witness BL, during this time period that you were in the -- that you were sleeping in the secondary school in Prozor in July, 1993, where were you taken to work?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Sometimes they would take us to Crni Vrh and at other times to Jurici, and once I myself went to Pisvir towards Jablanica.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: And when you were taken to Crni Vrh or Jurici or Pisvir towards Jablanica, what type of work were you performing?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Would were just digging all the time. We dug communications trenches, that sort of thing.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: And to follow up on a question by Judge Trechsel, at any time were you paid for this labour that you did?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, of course not, people. I never received a dinar. Never saw a dinar from 1992 until the war ended.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Now --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Excuse me. You said you were picked because you were young. Were those that were picked asked whether they were prepared to go? Did you have a choice?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, we did not have a choice. Nobody asked us whether we wanted to go or not. They would just point a finger at us and say, "You," and that would be it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Have you ever witnessed an incident where someone refused to go or made problems, and what happened, if that happened at all?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In my classroom, in the classroom that I was in, that kind of thing didn't happen.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In that secondary school, when you spent the night there did they give you anything to eat?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] As far as food was concerned, the women and children would bring us food from home. So they let them do that. And anybody who didn't have anyone to bring them any food, they would give them some bread and some tins.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could you flee?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, we couldn't, because there was --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the witness repeat his answer, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] During the night when you were asleep, you were under the supervision of armed soldiers, were you? Were you locked in, in the classrooms?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't know. There was a guard at the door, at the entrance to the school building, but nobody locked the classrooms, because we had to go to the toilet, for example.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You said there was a guard and there were 500 of you. You couldn't overpower the guard and escape?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, we weren't armed and the guard was armed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Witness BL, at this point in time in July, 1993, what armed force controlled the town of Prozor?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: In 1993, you mean?

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Yes, July. July, 1993, the period you were at the secondary school. What force, military force, controlled the town of Prozor?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The HVO army controlled Prozor.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Now, the -- during the time that you were in the secondary school in Prozor in July, 1993, what were the ages of the men that were taken to work?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They were the young men, and when they used up all the young men then what was left also came in handy.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Can you give us an approximation of what you mean by "the young men," or what was left? When you say "what was left," can you give us an approximate range of ages?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, they were young people of 20, 30. They were the strongest and youngest, the 20-year-olds and 30-year-olds.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Witness BL, you told us earlier that you were at the secondary school in Prozor until 31 July, 1993. What happened on that day?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: On the 31st of July, 1993, early in the morning two or three shells fell. One fell near the school building. Another one fell round about Viteks, and another about Unis, which is in the same area more or less. And the shell, and this is something we learnt from them, came from the BH army position.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Sorry, Witness BL. When you say, "This is something we learned from them," who do you mean by "them"?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Those people there. Those who were there with us. They said the armija had shelled. The guards and the other people there said that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: So you were told this by the guards --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: -- That it was -- okay.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Now, after these shells or grenades fell in the vicinity of the secondary school in Prozor, what did you do?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Two or three soldiers entered, I don't know exactly how many, and went round the classrooms, and one of them came to my classroom and he said, "We need people to work, 70 people." And then they selected one, two, three. They would say, "You, you, and you." They would single out the people, and then we'd go out. And at the entrance to the school, at the gate there, there was a man who made a list. I stepped out, and when I came up to him I knew him a little bit, so I asked him -- well, I knew his -- I didn't know his name and surname, but I knew him by sight. We would meet in Prozor. Anyway, I asked him where we were going, and he said, "I don't know." And we boarded the trucks. There were 20 to a truck and sometimes 50 to a truck. Twenty if one truck and 50 in the other. And I was in the truck with the 50 men.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: And where were you taken?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They took us in the direction of Makljen. And when we arrived at Makljen, they stopped a while, and there's a cafe called Baba Janja's cafe at Makljen and the truck stayed there with the 20 people, where always the 50 of us were driven off towards Crni Vrh.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: How far is it, Witness, from Makljen to Crni Vrh?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, I really don't know. How do you expect me to know that? I never measured the distance. I really don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Can you tell us what happened after you were driven off towards Crni Vrh?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We drove towards Crni Vrh as far as they were able to go with the vehicles, and then they stopped the truck and told us to get out, and they ordered us to move two by two, to march in a column two by two on foot, and that's what we did. We continued walking. And then you could hear a lot of noise and shouting in the woods, but we didn't dare turn round to see what was going on, because we were ordered to look down at ground, not to look up. And when we arrived, we got to a meadow, a small one. They ordered us to take our shoes and socks off and to throw all that onto a heap away from us, to the side of us, and that's what we did.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: After you did this, Witness BL, after you took off your shoes and socks and threw them in a heap, did you go anywhere else?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Then we continued walking towards the front line, and we learnt at the time that the BH army had taken control of positions -- this taken control of HVO positions at Crni Vrh. So we moved towards the -- towards where we were going. When we came close to, they stopped us and told us to look at the sun. So we stood there looking at the sun. And then they started mistreating us.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: What do you mean, Witness BL, by mistreating you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, one of them seemed to recognise me and said to me -- am I under protection now, under protective measures?

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Yes, but if you need, Witness BL, to mention name, then we need to go into private session.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. Let's go into private session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We're back in open session, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Witness BL, on this day when you were up on Makljen and Crni Vrh, in that area, was your brother part of the group that was with you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, he was.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Now, after you were put at the front or towards the front of this line, can you tell us what happened?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I'm not clear what you mean.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Well, just a moment ago you told us, and this is line 25 of page 27, "He ordered me to go to the head of the column, and I assumed that that meant at the front of the column to be killed." Did you in fact go to the head of the column?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. I had to abide by every order.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: And, Witness BL, after you got to the front of the column, tell us what happened.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They provoked us. They told a man to call out, "Allahu Akbar," and he did that. He said that. And then they would abuse him and say, "Why are you saying things like that when this is Croatian land?" And then they would tie us up. They tied us up with a wire, with a telephone wire. It's a strong wire. They tied us up. They tied our hands behind our backs like they do to prisoners. And I can't explain this, but they tied us round our next, too, so that if we were to fidget, the wire would pull tight. So we had to stand in line one by one, shoulder to shoulder, piled up like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Witness BL, just so that the record is clear, you've described being tied up. Who tied you up?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The HVO soldiers?

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: And again, sir, how do you know they were HVO soldiers?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, because we saw their insignia. There was nobody else there at that time. Who else could it be? Who else would tie us up? Nobody else came. Nobody else came from some other part of the world.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: And, Witness BL, approximately how many of you were tied up in this fashion on this day?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, the group of 50 men arrived there, and the other group, the group of 20 men, stayed at Makljen. I don't know where these 20 went in that truck, because they -- as I said, they loaded us up into two trucks.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Mr. President, with your leave I would ask that the witness be provided with a piece of paper, a blank piece of paper and a pen. I'm going to ask him if he can perhaps draw us a picture of how these -- these people were tied together. If that could please be put on the ELMO.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Now, Witness BL, I would ask if you could to please give us -- or make a drawing for us of the way if which the men that you were -- that were tied together were put in a line.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Marks].

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Okay. Now, sir, if you could -- thank you for that. Could you please just describe for us what it is you've drawn. What does this picture depict?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: On this picture you can see exactly -- well, you can see the upper line with the arrow. That's how our necks were tied. And the lower line is how our hands were tied behind our back. And the arrow represents the head of the column. And I was one of the first three men, or four. I was second or third. I'm not quite sure.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Now, sir, can you tell us in which direction this line was moving? And again, you'll need to draw on the piece of paper, sir, if you could. Draw on the paper the direction the line was moving.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Marks].

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Now, sir, next to the arrow -- next to the arrow in the direction the column was moving, could you please -- could you please place the number 1.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Marks].

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Now, Witness BL, if you could, please, could you indicate approximately where on your drawing the front line that you were moving towards was located.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Marks].

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Now, next to the front line that you've drawn, sir, if you could please place -- well, let me ask you this. What military force was on that front line?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: At that front line the BH army had that night taken control, and now the object was to regain positions lost.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Could you please, sir, place the letters ABH along the front line that the ABiH was holding on this day at the end of July, 1993.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Marks].

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Now, Witness BL, at this point in time when the line was moving or the column was moving towards the ABiH line, where were the HVO forces that were guarding the column?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Marks].

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Now, again, sir, this column that you've drawn where the prisoners were, approximately how many people were in that column?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: There were 50 of us prisoners. I've already said that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Could you please, sir, put the number 50 next to the little stick people that you've drawn so that we can all remember that there were 50 figures or 50 people along that column.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Marks].

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, sir, I would ask if you could please put the letters BL on the bottom right of that sheet and today's date, which is 31/8/2006, please. On the lower right-hand corner.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Marks].

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Thank you, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We have a question from the Judges.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MINDUA
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, just an explanation with respect to your picture. You drew the column with the people, and you said that there were about 50 people. Now, the others behind that first line that I see there, were they behind or were they along the same column? Because if I understood you correctly, this line was facing the front line of the BH army, and behind these people you had the HVO. So at one point you said that you were two by two, in a column of two by two, but were you one behind each other or two by two or what?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We were moving along here one by one in a column. You can see the arrow denoting the direction we were moving in. And -- but until we were tied up, we moved two by two. But once they'd tied us up, we were moving one by one.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: I note the time, Mr. President. This would be an appropriate spot for the break. I don't have much longer, perhaps 10 or 15 minutes after the break and we'll be completed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. We're going to take the break. It's 10.30. We reconvene at 10 to 11.00.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We'll now resume. Mr. Mundis.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Witness BL, right at the time we were taking the break I believe you'd completed drawing the diagram. Once the group of prisoners was tied together with the telephone wire, can you tell us what happened once the line was all tied together? What happened next?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We moved forward, as you can see in the sketch. We moved forward in the direction of the armija line, whereas the HVO soldiers killed the men one by one, killed the men who were lined up with us. And when someone fell down to the ground, the wire round our neck would be tightened and we would all fall down. We could not remain standing because we couldn't breathe. And then one of the HVO soldiers ordered one of the prisoners who was tied up in the line to do something. He untied him, and he ordered him to remove the dead bodies and to carry them about a hundred metres away behind us and behind the HVO soldiers. He was then to return to the end of the column and then stand there with his hands behind him. That's how things proceeded for a while, and we moved forward in this way. As we moved forward, the HVO soldier established a sort of line. At one point in time they dispersed to the side, and this soldier, one of the soldiers, turned us around himself so that we noticed that there was only one man in the vicinity, and this young man who was untying the dead and wounded jumped on the HVO soldier from behind. He took his rifle from him, pointed it at his throat. That's what I saw. I didn't see anything else. I don't know how I managed to untie my hands, but I used my hands to untie the wire around my neck. I don't know about how I managed to untie my hands. Perhaps I cut the wire. But anyway, I ran towards the BH army line. And in the meantime, they were no longer there. They must have already withdrawn from those positions, because there were relatives of ours, brothers of ours, of the men who were in the line. And later we find out that they had withdrawn. Everyone called out to their own. They recognised some of us, in fact. And I then went on, because there was a Croatian village down below, the village of Dobrasin, and there was a village the village of Boljkovac next to that village, and there was a demarcation line between those two villages. I went through the woods, and while fleeing I broke my left arm when I -- I then fell to the -- I broke my left arm when I fell to the ground. Finally I reached the village of Voljavac, and we were taken to the primary school in Voljavac. That's where we were received. On the following day we were seen by a doctor there, and he sent me to the military hospital in Jablanica. He referred me to that hospital.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Witness BL, I'm -- let me interrupt you here. I have some follow-on questions from what you've just described for us. You told us on page 33, line 12, 12 and 13, you said, "At one point in time they dispersed to the side." Can you tell us, at that point in time what the HVO soldiers were doing? The ones who had been behind you, what were they doing?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I have or already told you, but I don't know whether you've understood me. The line they were taking as we were advancing was being established extended to the side, and they then dispersed, and only one soldier remained with us. We're not talking about kilometres. It was 50 metres or so. I didn't take a metre to measure the distance, but the ground is very difficult. It's not flat ground.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Again, sir, perhaps I've misunderstood or it's not clear to me, but where at this point in time were the rest of the HVO soldiers who had been behind you? Where did they go, if you saw where they went? Can you tell us, please?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The men behind us would leave and take up positions to the side.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Now, sir, you've told us about this lone HVO soldier that was overpowered. What was the reaction, if any, from the other HVO soldiers in the area as this lone HVO soldier was overpowered?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: They didn't react at that point in time, but at the point we started running they fired at us. But since the ground is very difficult, since it's not accessible, we ran down the hill and there was a forest there so they couldn't do anything to us. Twenty-seven of us fled at that point in time. Twenty-three remained behind us. Some of them were dead, some wounded. We didn't know exactly what the situation was. We weren't doctors, so this wasn't possible for us.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Now --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: I'm sorry. Could the witness -- could you explain why you can give this figure so precisely?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, because when we arrived in the village, we made a count of the men who about there. We made a list, and we knew each other. And as there had been 50 of us, it was possible for us to determine who was present and who was absent. Whereas the young men who untied the men and put them to the side knew approximately how many people he had left up there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Hvala Lepa.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You say there were 50 of you tied up to each other. There was this telephone line that had been used to tie you up. It was around your necks and around your legs and your hands were tied up, and at one point in time the HVO opened fire, and 27 of you fled. Fifty minus 27 means that when fire was opened at the beginning there were 23 of your comrades who were shot or were killed. Could you provide us with any more precise information? Since there were 50 of you initially, in fact how many survivors were there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Twenty-seven of us survived, whereas 23 men had been hit at various points in time. It didn't all happen at the same time. They weren't all killed at the same time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you for that explanation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: You have just spoken of the time element. Do you have an idea? Can you tell us how long it took between the moment your line was set into motion towards the enemy or towards the armija and the time that you managed to flee? How long was that, a quarter of an hour, five minutes, an hour?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, we set off from the school in the morning. We headed for the hill. And in the evening, at 7.00 p.m., approximately, well, that's the time we fled.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Excuse --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That was just prior to the aksa, as they say.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Excuse me. I have not expressed myself clearly enough. I am only wondering about the time when you were first exposed to the fire of the other side, when the line that you have drawn started moving towards ABiH.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't know. We didn't have any watches on us. I don't know whether it was at noon or at some other time. I couldn't really say.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's correction: The witness didn't say prior to the action. He said prior to the aksa, which is the Bosnian term -- or Bosniak term for evening prayer.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Witness BL, you mentioned again, and for the purpose of everyone in the courtroom, page 33, lines 2 and 3 -- or 1, 2, and 3 on page 33, you said, "We moved forward in the direction of the armija line, whereas the HVO soldiers killed the men one by one, killed the men who were lined up with us." How do you know, Witness BL, that it was the HVO soldiers who killed the men that were in the line or in the column with you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, people I'm telling you that they killed the mean one by one. They weren't all killed at the same time. But I know the man who was next to me. He was killed. This young man untied him. I saw him with my very own eyes. I saw the bullet hit him from behind. He wasn't hit from the front.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: At any point in time, sir, did you actually see the ABiH soldiers on the line that you were advancing towards?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, we didn't see them.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Did you hear any gunfire coming from the direction in front of you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: As we arrived there, no, there was no gunfire in front of us.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Perhaps, Mr. President, if we could briefly move into private session.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We're in open session, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Now that we're in open session, the cross-examination will now commence, and I'll give the floor to the first Defence team now.

utterances.speaker: MS. TOMANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The Defence of Dr. Prlic has no questions for this witness. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. For the parties' information, the Prosecution has used up one hour, 15 minutes. Mr. Murphy?

utterances.speaker: MR. MURPHY
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... No questions for this witness thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. Murphy. Mr. Kovacic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I do have some questions for this witness. I believe I can get through them in 15 or 20 minutes depending on the answers.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Mr. BL. Unfortunately, I have to use these initials.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Before I give you the floor, we forgot or, rather, Mr. Mundis forgot to ask to tender the drawing or for it to be assigned a number.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. I believe that would be IC 00033. We would ask that that be admitted into evidence. We would also ask for the record that the two photographs shown to the witness, P 9683 and P 9685, be admitted into evidence as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. So those three documents have been admitted and recognised by the witness. Mr. Registrar, would you tell me whether IC 00033 has been admitted?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, it has been admitted.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] As well as P 9684 [as interpreted] and P 9685?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, they have all been admitted, P 09683, P 9685, IC 32, and IC 33.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Counsel Kovacic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. BL. I regret I have to address you with these initials, but that's the procedure. My name is Bozidar Kovacic. I am an attorney-at-law, and am acting for one of the accused, General Praljak. I will put a few questions to you. Let me first tell you that we both speak the same language, so I must ask you to always pause a little and leave time for the interpretation after my question, and I will do the same after your response. You'll see how this works. First let me put a few introductory questions to you to put this whole situation in context, the situation in July, 1993, when you were imprisoned and when you were digging trenches. Mr. BL, you told us that your family came to visit you in the school, brought you food, that there was some 500 men there, so you did get some information about what was going on. Isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No. We couldn't get any information because they would just come to the door where there was a guard and handover what they had brought.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: But did you men discuss among yourselves the rumours you had heard?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, the only rumours we could hear was from HVO members while we were working.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: At that time did you know or did you learn that in the last few days of July, 1993, Bugojno had fallen and that as a consequence of the fall of Bugojno about 20.000 refugees from the Bugojno area arrived in the area of Prozor, the area where you lived? Did you hear anything about this?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I didn't. I couldn't have. Who could I hear it from? We didn't have any radio or television.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: But you said you talked to the HVO soldiers.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, yes, a little. They told us what they could, but we didn't discuss politics.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Did any of these HVO soldiers tell you he was a refugee from Bugojno?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't know. They didn't say that to me.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Mr. BL, in response to His Honour's question, you said that you recognised one of the escorts on the truck. You said that he was in Bosnia. Is Bugojno part of Bosnia according to the way you say that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I didn't say whether or not he was a refugee, but his accent gave me that impression. However, he might have been a migrant or a refugee.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Very well. Well, just to be sure that you know nothing about this, maybe you will know something about the following: Did you hear that after Bugojno fell about 3.000 HVO soldiers who had to leave that area arrived in Prozor and some of them were armed? Did you hear anything about that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No. I had no media available to me. I couldn't hear anything about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Did you hear that in Prozor and the surrounding villages there was quite a lot of chaos because of the loss of the HVO positions and the large number of refugees?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I was in prison. I wasn't free, so how could I know about that?

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Witness BL, but you weren't completely isolated. You did get news. That's what I'm putting to you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, please explain to me how. How could I get news, do you know?

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Well, I'm the one putting questions here, but I'll tell you. News reached you because people from the village came to bring you food. Some people were allowed to go home for various reasons. The guards talked to you. You went to work, and some people did talk to you while you were there. So little by little, news reached you, and it was quite natural that the rumours should be passed around among you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That's not correct as far as I'm concerned. Nobody talked to me, nor did I know anything about this.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: So you say you knew nothing about this chaos and this huge number of refugees; is that correct? Could you say whether it's correct that you heard nothing about this?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No. I heard nothing about it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Very well. Later on when you returned to your village after all the things you unfortunately experienced, did you hear about that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, I still haven't gone back to my village.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Did you go for a visit?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Maybe once in a year, but I never discussed those things.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: But you socialised with your relatives, with your fellow villagers. You had contacts with them. Did you hear these things from them later on?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, I'll tell you now. There were 60 households in my village. There are only 15 or less now. So who could I have contacts with?

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Very well. I'll move on. But you're saying that neither in July, 1993, nor subsequently did you learn that this huge number of refugees arrived in the area around Prozor and in Prozor itself, and that because of the fighting there was chaos there in July. You're saying you never learned that; correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I didn't learn that. Nobody told me anything about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Very well. It's enough for you to say whether it's correct or not. You told us about the situation at Crni Vrh where you were taken to dig trenches, and you yourself said that the BH army had taken Crni Vrh; correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. I heard that they had taken it that night. I didn't see it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Very well. You are a local man. You had seven military training. In view of the training you received in the JNA before the war, can you confirm whether or not it's correct that Crni Vrh is an elevation and that the person or the army holding Crni Vrh is in control of Prozor? Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: So in military terms it's an important elevation. Do we agree?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: You said that you were taken to dig trenches at Pidris.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I never mentioned Pidris.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: I may have misunderstood. Was it Pisvir?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Pisvir, yes, in the direction of Jablanica.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Can you repeat the name again?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: P-i-s-v-i-r, Pisvir.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Very well. You yourself said that Pisvir is in the direction of Jablanica going from Prozor.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Do you agree that's 6 or 7 kilometres away from Jablanica?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It could be, I didn't measure the distance. If you go Gracac along a macadam road up a hill the village of Gracac is there.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: And new trenches were dug there again; right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, that's right. Trenches were dug there.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: The HVO dug trenches?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We prisoners dug the trenches for the HVO soldiers.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: And what army were these trenches facing?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I assume the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina, because there were no Serbs in the area.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: So this was in the operations for taking terrain towards the south, towards Jablanica?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: And it was the BH army that was conquering the territory, and the areas of Jablanica and Prozor were to be put under the control of the army.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, the HVO, because the army was in Jablanica.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: But you said just a moment ago that the armija had taken them at Crni Vrh overlooking Prozor?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. Crni Vrh, yes, but that's a different period, Pisvir.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: When were the trenches at Pisvir dug?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We went to Jurici, we went to Crni Vrh. We went to Pisvir. I should have carried down a notebook with me and noted down the days and places where we were but we couldn't do that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Well, that's quite clear. Of course I'm not asking you that. It's quite clear that I don't expect that, but we will agree that all this took place in July, 1993?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, in July while I was at the secondly school. That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Very well. Thank you very much. You said that from the school they took you to work in several places, and you said this was done by the HVO and that you saw the insignia. Were these HVO insignia or HVO military police insignia?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: HVO. The police didn't go to the line. We all know what the police does.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: While you were at these locations, especially Crni Vrh but also the others you mentioned, did you see any additional insignia? Do you know what HVO unit this was?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No. I don't understand these things. What was important to us was that it was the HVO. That was the Croatian army, as far as we were concerned, and whether they had a bird some other emblem or what kind of brigade it was, we weren't interested in that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: So you didn't see any additional insignia apart from HVO?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No. I don't know about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: It says in the record that it was the Croatian army. Did you ever see the army that came from -- an army that came from Croatia there? You mean the HVO?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I meant the HVO. That's what we say when we say that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: And these HVO soldiers, let me ask you the following: Did you see any people you knew by sight among them?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, when we were working we didn't dare look people in the eye, look at them directly. Well, of course we knew some people, but I'd rather avoid them if I can, because I was afraid.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Is it correct, then, that some of them were local people? Yes or no?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Well, let's move on and go back to some other issues you raised. I'm going back to the very beginning of your testimony with regard to the existence of the Territorial Defence. You said that you were mobilised by the Territorial Defence. I put an additional question to you about that. Is it correct that the full and official name of that institution was the municipal Territorial Defence Staff in Prozor? Correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I think that's correct, but I don't know if it's the Municipal Staff or not. I'm not that educated. I don't understand these things.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: In any case, you got the call-up papers in Prozor?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, in writing. I got that at home, that I should report to the TO. I reported, and they put me in a vehicle and they took me to the Rama hydroelectric power plant, the dam on the lake, and there they gave me a uniform and weapons.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Very well. At the time while you were there, were all able-bodied men from the municipality called up?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, they were. I don't know whether they all received the call-up papers at the same time. I can't talk about the entire municipality.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Very well. Did Croats and Muslims alike receive call-up papers?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, of course they did. I know that we were up there and that there were both Croats and Muslims there. I can't say anything different.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Do you agree that in 1992 the Territorial Defence had that Joint Command you mentioned?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That's what people said. I don't know. I don't know whether it was joint at the top or not. We were told it was a Joint Command. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Very well. You mentioned going to the lines after mobilisation and that you were there in shifts. You said that in 1992 you worked in shifts 15 days on, 15 days off.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, whether it was 15 or 7 days, it wasn't always the same. It varied depending on the number of men.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: While we fully agree, and in 1993 when you were at Idovac, at the positions with the HVO there were shifts there too; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Before you were called up, just before you were called up, were you employed?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Where did you work, if I may ask that?

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: When you were mobilised did your employment cease?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: So would spend 7 or 15 days on a shift. I'm speaking about the period when you were in the Territorial Defence. And when you were off duty, you went home; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: You didn't go to any barracks.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No. No, we didn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: When you were at home, you were a free man so to speak?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Of course.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: You had no military duties when you were off duty?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Do we agree that during those 7, 10, or 15 days when you were off duty you were a civilian?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, yes. Yes, I was.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: And did you bring your rifle home from the front line?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, until Prozor fell. Until the 23rd of October, 1992. After that, we didn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Very well. Mr. BL, is it correct or do you know that in early 1992 when many people felt that war was coming to Bosnia, that there would a Serbian aggression, regardless of the fact that people had different opinions, did many people buy weapons with their own money, weapons to defend themselves from an impending attack from the Serbs?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, whoever could did.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just a moment, please. Mr. Murphy.

utterances.speaker: MR. MURPHY
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... private session for just a moment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We're back in open session, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise for that slip, but I didn't feel that it would indicate the witness's identity because it's a large employer employing several hundred employees.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Witness, let's carry on where we left off. You have understood the reason for this interruption. It was so that your identity should not be disclosed. Anyway, you confirmed and said that some people, although you don't know their names and surnames, but you agree that many people purchased weapons in early 1992 with their own money; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't know if it's correct or not. Some people did, others didn't. I did hear that people were buying weapons, but I didn't see it myself, so I can't confirm whether it was actually correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: All right. Fine. Now, you yourself, you as BL, did you purchase any weapons for defence?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No. I received an M-48 rifle and ten bullets. You know where. I've already told you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Well, perhaps you are aware that that weaponry for the Territorial Defence was procured, among others, by the HVO.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Perhaps, but I really couldn't say. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: All right. Fine. Now, in 1993 when went to take up your shift at Idovac, they issued weapons to you again there, did they not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: And you said that you left the weapons at the positions there when you were off shift.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes. There was a shed there, and we would leave it there.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: And that was the rule for all people taking up their shifts except for people who owned their own weapons.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't know. I don't know about that rule. I know that we Muslims who had a special shed where we slept, we one hand over our weapons. I don't know what other people did. We didn't spend the night together, so I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: You don't know. You don't know whether the HVO soldiers or some up at the line also left their weapons there?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I didn't know that. We didn't go to their part. We would go to our part of the village and they would go to theirs.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Now, when your shift was completed and you went home and left your weapons, another soldier came up to take up are position, the other shift.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, of course.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: So your replacement, if I can put it that way, who took up your shift used the weapons left up at the line.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, I don't know. We would take it back to the warehouse. Now, who would issue it out again, I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: And when you come back again, you were issued the weapon again?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Thank you. There was -- we had our interruption, and you were saying that when you weren't on shift in 1992, when you weren't doing your shift in 1992 in the village, did you engage in any other work? Because the factory had closed down, did you do any other work to earn money?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, of course it was closed. It was shut down and we only had farming.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: So they considered you to be a civilian. The Territorial Defence didn't say you're soldier, you're not allowed to work?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Well, no, nobody prevented us from working. Of course not.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: I just have a very small question to ask. Witness BL, when you said you were imprisoned in the school, you mentioned a man who made lists of your named when you were loaded up onto trucks. You said you knew him by sight, and you asked him whether he knew where they were taking you. He said he did not know. Do you happen to know his name?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I said straight away he didn't happen to know his name. We just knew each other by sight when passing, in passing. We would happen to pass each other in town. We would say, "Hi, how are you?" That kind of thing.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, may we go back into private session for just one moment, please, because I'd like to put a name to the witness and the name is on the witness list.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Registrar, private session, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We're back in open session, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation].

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Witness BL, you said in your introduction that you had some military training on a recoilless gun during the Yugoslav People's Army days, the JNA.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't know what you mean. What does that mean?

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Well, I apologise. I wasn't precise enough. When you did your service in the Yugoslav People's Army a long before this war broke out, you were engaged in training for a recoilless gun; is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, that is right.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: So you do have some knowledge of weapons.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
