utterances.text: So as a soldier who knew this subject matter, would you agree that if we only have mortars at Crni Vrh it is Prozor that is the target, or within range, that Prozor is within range?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Do you know how long the line, demarcation line between the BH army and the HVO, was maintained? When did the army -- when the army took control of Crni Vrh, what happened to the HVO?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't know. I wasn't there. When we were brought there, there were soldiers in the woods, and then we would move around. We would move towards the front line where we had been digging trenches beforehand. So when we reached those trenches, we fled. That's what happened. I don't want to repeat everything that happened, the whole incident.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: So the HVO line had already fallen when you arrived up there.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: The BH army was already in control of that area; is that right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That completes my cross-examination. I have no further questions for this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: May I just --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The Judges have some questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Just one small question. I'm not sure that I know what the recoilless gun is, the weapon you have been trained on. What is that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I don't know how to explain it to you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Is it a gun you use to shoot at armoured vehicles?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It is an anti-armour gun, yes, an anti-armour gun. I said when I testified a recoilless gun is used against armoured vehicles, so I was in the anti-armour unit in the JNA.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Is it mainly a tube in which you place a rocket about a foot long and then shoot that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It's a tube which has two -- it's on a stand with two vehicles, and it is manned by five individuals. Two wheels, sorry. Two wheels, interpreter's correction. The shells are placed in the rear end and they come out through the front end.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE TRECHSEL
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. A follow-up question. The Defence said that after Bugojno there was chaos. Now, when you dug trenches and when you left the secondary school to the trenches, and on the road along the route were there any HVO checkpoints? Did the HVO stop the trucks you were in to see who was inside or not, or did you go directly from the school building to the location where you were trench digging, and you weren't stopped by anyone along the way?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Nobody stopped us anywhere. We went directly -- well, not quite directly, but as far as a vehicle could go and reach the line where the digging was taking place.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Now, the day you were at Makljen and the day you left the secondary school in the morning in order to be in that column of 50 men, Makljen is to the north of Prozor and to go from Prozor to Makljen you have to take a winding road, and the distance is approximately 10 kilometres. Now, along that road, on your way there, did the truck keep going or did it stop at any point?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, nobody stopped it. It might have stopped for a few minutes by the Baba Janja cafe. I don't know what for. But we were under the canvas, under the tarpaulin, so I couldn't see what was going on. But it just stopped for a short while there and continued on its way.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Counsel Alaburic.

utterances.speaker: MS. ALABURIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour. Cross-examination by. Ms. Alaburic:

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, my name is Vesna Alaburic. I'm an attorney from Zagreb and I'm here as Defence counsel for General Milivoj Petkovic. I haven't prepared any questions to ask you but I would like to ask you something with respect to your testimony here today, so I do have a few questions because some of your statements are not quite clear to me, and I can't paint a picture of everything you told us today. Now, to start off, you told us that your brother was in the truck with the 50 men who were --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Can we go into private session, please?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Let's move into private session.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We're in open session, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We have another ten minutes before the break. Ms. Tomic, you have the floor. MS. TOMASEGOVIC TOMIC: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. Cross-examination by Ms. Tomasegovic Tomic:

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good day, sir. My name is Dijana Tomasegovic Tomic, and I remember Mr. Valentin Coric in this case. I know it's difficult for you to look back to all of these events, so I will try to be very brief. I will try to put brief and clear questions to you by which you can answer yes or no. Sir, today you told us that throughout the period of these events the military police only spent one night with you in the fire brigade in Prozor, whereas for the remainder of the time the HVO or other members or soldiers of the HVO were with you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: I'd now like to go back to the night spent in the fire station, and I have a few questions about that. Were you beaten by the members of the military police that night or were you abused in any other way?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I personally wasn't, but I didn't hear or see anything either.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Tell me, did the military policemen threaten you that night?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I wasn't threatened.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: And I only have one more question for you. Did the military policemen interrogate you that night?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, nor did I see any interrogations.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much, sir. MS. TOMASEGOVIC TOMIC: [Interpretation] At that concludes my cross-examination. Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And the next member of the Defence team, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. IBRISIMOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. I don't have any questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Ms. Nozica, Mr. Murphy, no questions?

utterances.speaker: MR. MURPHY
utterances.text: No, we have no questions, Your Honour. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Everyone has put their questions to the witness. Mr. Mundis, any re-examination?

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Just very briefly on one point, Mr. President, that arose from the cross-examination by counsel for Mr. Praljak that I'm referring to specifically page 54, line 12, and page 57, line 25.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Witness BL, do you recall the specific date that you were demobilised from the military?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Please repeat that question. I haven't understood it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: You told us, sir, that at a certain time in April, 1992, you received call non-papers and were, therefore, mobilised; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Did you ever receive any type of official paper or documents telling you that you were demobilised, that is, that you were released from being a member of the Territorial Defence?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: No, I didn't receive anything.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: We have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Sir, this completes your testimony, and on behalf of the Judges I would like to thank you for coming to have testified at The Hague. I wish you a safe trip home. Before you leave, I'll ask the usher to lower the blinds.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We have a few more minutes. Perhaps we could conclude a little later, but, Mr. Mundis, as far as Monday is concerned, our schedule is the schedule that was announced a few days ago; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: That is correct, Mr. President. The witness that's scheduled for Monday will be here and will commence what I believe the Chamber has indicated would be five days of testimony.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. As we have already said, the witness will be examined over a two-day period by the Prosecution, after which the Defence will have three days for their cross-examination, and we hope, as I said yesterday, that Defence counsel will manage to reach an agreement on how to use their time. If you fail to reach such an agreement, inform us of the fact and we will decide on how to deal with the matter, but we hope that you will reach a decision on how to divide the time amongst yourselves. Mr. Registrar, perhaps we could raise the blinds now as the witness has left the courtroom. Are there any issues that any of the parties would like to raise? Mr. Mundis?

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: The Prosecution has nothing for today, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Praljak. The computer, I assume? THE ACCUSED PRALJAK: [Interpretation] No. I still don't have a computer, which is difficult to understand, but I don't want to go on about this. It would show a lack of dignity, if I can put it in that way, but there is something I wanted to say about testimony given in closed session. The UN Security Council established the Tribunal, and the purpose of establishing it was to contribute to the establishment of peace in Bosnia and Herzegovina and beyond, in the territory of the western Balkans. It's not possible to attain such peace in the truth is no determined able to get the peace unless truth is determined and we are trying to determine the truth, here. It's important though in order to establish truth that the witnesses who testify here accept the burden of testifying. Bosnia-Herzegovina has -- peace has been present in Bosnia and Herzegovina for a long time, and I don't think there are any more risks, any more threats there. So I regret the fact that witnesses testify in closed session or in private session because it is necessary for what this witness has just said to be publicly accessible. It must also be accessible in Rama, in Prozor, which is where he is from so people could know exactly what happened, how these things happened, so they could know the main actors so at that justice can function, so that indictments can be issued if necessary, so that one could paint a coherent picture of everything and realise who is responsible for what, so that the sense of the events could be understood. Thus having established what the truth is one could contribute to the peace. But people are hiding behind their own cowardice and while doing so they believe that they can also tell lies because they are protected for -- if they hadn't testified in closed session these lies would have come to light. If a witness is here and wants to testify truthfully, then such witnesses have to accept the burden of giving such testimony. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It's according to the Rules of this Tribunal that one has protective measures for witnesses and all the Trial Chambers of the Tribunal act in this manner. If a witness requests protective measures, whatever the reasons may be, personal, subjective, et cetera, we decide to grant these measures or not to grant them. In the previous case, you noted that the protective measures granted weren't complete. We granted the previous witness partial protective measures. Mr. Mundis, I see that you're on your feet.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUNDIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. Again for the record the Prosecution objects to this type of argumentation and these types of outburst by the accused Mr. Praljak. For him to suggest at this point that a witness is lying because this Chamber has granted protective measures is outrageous and also to suggest that it's cowardice that brings these witnesses or is the source for these witnesses to request protective measures is out of line with, all due respect to Mr. Praljak. It takes a great deal of courage for these witnesses to come and testify in this courtroom and for him to suggest otherwise is inappropriate.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [No interpretation].

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, since my client mentioned this, I would like to inform the Chamber this computer story has been going on since April. I've provided copies of the correspondence exchanged. You have an idea of the problem. But over the last four days I believe that I have exchanged two e-mails with the person responsible within the registry and now questions have been raised about software. They say that in about two weeks' time they might have the hardware but --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The legal officer has informed me that next week your client will have doubled the memory of his computer and the solution will be dealt with next week.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If I may just say one sentence. I understand the objection as a matter of principle that my colleague made, but I don't see how one could interpret what my client said as saying that the witness is a coward. I don't see how one could interpret his words as meaning he had lied. He quite simply didn't say that. THE ACCUSED PRALJAK: [Interpretation] I don't know what the interpretation was but that is not what I said. I didn't say anything like that, not at that point in time. I only mentioned things as hypothesis or I put them in the conditional.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We take note of what you have said.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'd like to thank everyone, and we will reconvene on Monday at 2.15. I wish you a good weekend, and I will see you all on Monday.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Monday, the 4th day of September, 2006, at 2.15 p.m. 19 20 21 22 23 24 25
